stem:
A 6-year-old with asthma is using a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) without a spacer.

Why is a spacer recommended for children?

options.label: A
options.text: Enhances gastrointestinal absorption of swallowed medication by reducing particle size
options.explanation: A spacer is not used to improve gastrointestinal absorption. In fact, one benefit is that less medication impacts the oropharynx and gets swallowed.

options.label: B
options.text: Reduces the need for coordination between actuation and inhalation
options.explanation:
Correct. A spacer makes MDI use easier because the child does not need perfect timing between pressing the inhaler and inhaling.

That improves drug delivery to the lungs.

options.label: C
options.text: Increases the nominal medication dose released by each canister actuation
options.explanation: The dose metered by the canister is unchanged. A spacer can increase the fraction reaching the lungs, which is different from increasing the nominal dose per puff.

options.label: D
options.text: Improves delivery when several puffs are released into the chamber together
options.explanation: Use one puff at a time: multiple puffs together reduce effective delivery. The child then uses a slow inhalation with a breath hold, or several tidal breaths if needed.

options.label: E
options.text: Accelerates the rate of aerosol delivery by increasing particle velocity to the airways
options.explanation: A spacer actually slows the aerosol and reduces large-particle impaction in the oropharynx. It does not improve delivery by blasting particles faster into the airways.

context:
A spacer reduces the coordination needed between pressing a puffer and inhaling. It slows the aerosol so less deposits in the mouth and throat.

More of the metered dose can reach the lungs; the nominal dose released by the canister stays the same.

Give one puff at a time. Match the inhalation technique to the child’s ability and check technique regularly.
